title: Urda crash, ECB rate warning and November rail strikes

chapters.title: ECB rates and its next president

summary:
We examine the Urda rail crash investigation, compensation and the transport minister's forthcoming appearance in Congress. We also cover the ECB's December rate warning, November train strikes, pensions, Catalan property proposals, Zaragoza's European Green Capital award and Milei's planned Madrid visit.

Enjoying Spain Daily? Support us: https://buymeacoffee.com/spanified

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The central bank said no to higher rates yesterday. Is that good news?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Not really. Its president says a rise in December is more than likely. oh no

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Hold on. So what does that do to my monthly payment?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Good question. We'll answer it after the news.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Good morning. It's Friday, the thirtieth of October, and this is Spain Daily, from Spanified dot com!

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: I'm Inna, here with Dima. Today, November train strikes and a president's planned return to Madrid after insulting Spain's prime minister. Will they finally meet face to face?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: First, the Urda rail disaster: the investigation, payments for victims and their families, and questions facing the transport minister.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: La Vanguardia reports that the Urda crash in Toledo has killed sixty-nine people. Investigators estimate the AVE struck a stationary Iryo train at between a hundred and sixty and two hundred kilometres an hour. A signalling failure preceded the collision. Evidence collection continues, and key witnesses have yet to be interviewed.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Mandatory traveller insurance pays about seventy-two thousand euros to the heirs of each person killed, with separate payments for injuries, to be made quickly. Transport Minister Óscar Puente faces dismissal calls and will address Congress on November third.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Dima, who pays beyond that mandatory insurance, and how long could families have to wait?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The liability insurance of whoever is found responsible would apply separately. Those larger payments can take years.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Adif's main insurer, QBE Europe, also covers Iryo's liability. Who is responsible is still being investigated.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: What does the investigation say about the safety systems that should have prevented this?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Investigators say a signalling failure started that morning. After that, none of the necessary safety barriers worked.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Puente gives another press conference today, and appears in Congress on November third. Some allies and unions are calling for his dismissal, but Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has not dismissed him.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Borrowing costs stayed unchanged yesterday. Expansión reports that the European Central Bank held rates at two point five percent. President Christine Lagarde said a December increase is more than likely, although there is no fixed path. September inflation was well above the bank's target.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: So a pause, but not a relief. Why wait at all if a rise looks likely?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Government bond yields had already risen, making borrowing more expensive. right December brings another decision. A further rise would take the rate to two point seven five percent.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: I'd still take the pause. But variable mortgages follow Euribor. If rates rise in December, monthly payments can follow.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The bank's leadership is changing too. El País reports that Lagarde will leave on February seventh next year, almost nine months early. Former Spanish central bank governor Pablo Hernández de Cos and former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot lead the succession race. Experts put them almost neck and neck.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Does it matter who sits at the top, Inna? Rate decisions come from the Governing Council.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Maybe, but the ECB's decisions on borrowing cover the whole eurozone. mhm Eurozone states propose candidates, finance ministers pick one, and the European Council takes the final decision.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: So a Spaniard could win, but Spain does not decide. Lagarde's two colleagues leave too, so three posts are open.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Rail passengers face consecutive days of disruption in November. Heraldo reports that drivers' union Semaf has called a full-day Renfe strike on November tenth. Partial stoppages follow on November twelfth, surrounding the general strike on November eleventh. Semaf says safety negotiations have stalled; Renfe says it has met its commitments.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: What are the drivers saying hasn't happened, and what's Renfe's answer?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Semaf says meetings keep being postponed and a follow-up commission has not met. Renfe says it has carried out most of the measures and that the pending ones exceed its powers.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Three days in a row, then. And the drivers say it goes back to a February agreement that called off earlier strikes.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Infrastructure funding faces a separate constraint. Spain still uses its twenty twenty-three state budget after three extensions, Expansión reports. Former Court of Auditors president María José de la Fuente says unchanged funding doesn't absorb rising costs. She says this limits infrastructure improvements and maintenance.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: She also says uncertainty over state investment prevents regional and local authorities from planning their own projects. And the population has grown by at least four hundred thousand people, which adds to demand for public services.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Does this connect to the rail crashes at all?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The article links it to the fall in rail maintenance spending, which has been cited as a factor in this year's two high-speed rail tragedies.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For someone with a shorter working life in Spain, how many contribution years open the door to a pension?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Heraldo says you need at least fifteen years of contributions to get a retirement pension. If the pension falls short of the minimum, you can claim an income-tested top-up.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Fifteen years only? What would the monthly amount be?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The 2026 minimum is about eight hundred and ninety euros a month with no dependent spouse. It is higher with a dependent spouse.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Early retirement isn't allowed if the penalty would push the pension below the minimum that applies to you.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Zaragoza has something to celebrate. El País reports that the European Commission named it European Green Capital twenty twenty-eight. Mayor Natalia Chueca says the award recognises decades of climate policy. Sixty percent of city buses are electric, and two hundred and fifty thousand trees have been planted.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Oh, I like the trees more than the title. oh nice But does the award mean the heat problem is solved?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Far from it. Zaragoza had a very hot summer, with heat waves and tropical nights through most of June and July. Its award programme will focus on fighting climate change and adapting to it.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: I'd choose shade over a trophy. Those buses and trees are concrete changes, though, in a city facing serious summer heat.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: In Catalonia, the party Comuns wants home-purchase restrictions aimed at companies, funds and individuals owning five or more homes in stressed housing zones. El País reports that proposed amendments would exempt individuals below that threshold. The bill remains under negotiation, with a plenary vote expected in December.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The aim is limiting speculation, right? But does the regional government agree?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: It prefers regulating how homes are used rather than limiting sales. Comuns will register the amendments anyway and keep talking until the vote.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Madrid hosts the Ibero-American Summit on November fourth and fifth, bringing together leaders from twenty-two countries. El País says Argentine president Javier Milei plans to attend, according to Argentine government sources, pending official confirmation. His return follows insults aimed at Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez during a recent Madrid visit.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Does that put them face to face after Milei called Sánchez a dictator and a thief?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: It would. They haven't met face to face in any of his seven visits to Spain as president. Brazil's president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva might attend too, but that is unconfirmed.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And Lula's attendance is in doubt. Milei has refused to officially recognise his re-election, held on Sunday the twenty-fifth.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Coming up: Puente's press conference today and Congress on November third. Madrid's summit follows, then Renfe disruption from November tenth to twelfth.
